ChatGPT said:ChatGPT

That's a useful simplification. We don't need to model the entire Active Directory OU tree.

For this application, we only need to capture the bottom-level OU where the migration objects will be created.

I'd therefore model the two hierarchies differently:

Feature

Folder hierarchy

OU hierarchy

Number of levels

Configurable

Configurable

Input

Folder names

OU names

Structure

Sequential path

Parent-to-child path

Directory creation commands

Distinguished Name (DN) for the target OU

Scope

Domain-specific

Proposed OU interface

The engineer specifies the OU hierarchy, and the application constructs the target DN.

For example, using entirely fictional values:

Plain text
OU=Laboratory, OU=Equipment, OU=NewEnvironment, DC=example, DC=com

The application uses that DN when generating commands such as New-ADGroup or New-ADOrganizationalUnit where appropriate.

An important design decision

I'd avoid asking engineers to enter the same OU information repeatedly for every group.

Instead, capture the target OU once per migration/domain and reuse it throughout the generation process.

That reduces data entry and, more importantly, reduces the chance of generating commands against the wrong OU.

Our emerging design now has two configurable hierarchies: folders and target OUs, with independent numbers of levels.

Absolutely. I think we're now at the point where we can give Cursor a proper architectural brief rather than asking it to build something based on a loose description.

I'd approach this as Phase 1: Build the application foundation and dynamic input interface, without implementing the company-specific PowerShell generation rules yet.

There are three things I'd establish:

  1. A clear application architecture.

  2. A UI design that makes the migration process straightforward.

  3. A small set of living documentation files that prevent Cursor from making architectural decisions independently as the project evolves.

I'd also make sure we don't accidentally introduce AI, databases, authentication or unnecessary infrastructure.

1. Proposed application architecture

Migration Command Builder

Phase 1 architecture

Presentation layer

Dynamic forms, folder hierarchy, OU hierarchy, domain selection and command preview.

Application layer

Migration configuration, state management and orchestration.

Generation layer

Deterministic TypeScript functions and version-controlled PowerShell templates.

Output layer

PowerShell preview, copy to clipboard and file export.

Key architectural decisions

  • Folder hierarchy and OU hierarchy are independently configurable.

  • OU input captures the complete ancestry but targets the bottom-level OU.

  • Support two independently configured domains.

  • No fixed limit on hierarchy depth, other than a sensible UI limit.

  • No AI-generated PowerShell.

  • No execution of PowerShell from the application.

  • No database in the initial release.

  • Generation logic must be independent of the UI.

One additional consideration: the OU hierarchy should generate a Distinguished Name from its levels, rather than treating the OU names as a simple folder path.

2. UI reference image

I'd favour a clean engineering tool rather than an administration console. The engineer should be able to understand the migration structure at a glance, without navigating dozens of spreadsheet columns.

3. Cursor implementation prompt

I'd give Cursor the following prompt. It's deliberately prescriptive about scope so it doesn't run off and build features we haven't agreed on.

Writing

Project: Migration Command Builder

Phase 1 — Application Foundation

You are building a deterministic infrastructure migration command-generation application.

The objective is to replace a complicated Excel-based PowerShell command generator with a simpler, configurable web application.

1. Core principles

  • All PowerShell generation must use deterministic, hard-coded application logic.

  • Never use AI, LLMs or external AI services to generate commands.

  • Never execute PowerShell commands from the application.

  • The application generates commands for engineers to review, copy and subsequently execute on the appropriate servers.

  • Keep the architecture modular and easy to extend.

  • Prioritise functionality and simplicity over feature richness.

  • Do not introduce unnecessary infrastructure.

2. Technology

First inspect the existing repository and identify its current framework, dependencies and conventions.

If starting from scratch, use:

  • Next.js with App Router

  • React

  • TypeScript

  • Tailwind CSS

Use client-side state initially. Do not introduce a database, authentication, backend services or external APIs in Phase 1.

3. Application architecture

Separate the application into the following layers:

Presentation layer

  • Migration configuration interface.

  • Dynamic hierarchy inputs.

  • Domain configuration.

  • PowerShell command preview.

Application layer

  • Migration state and configuration.

  • Input orchestration.

  • Coordination of generation functions.

Generation layer

  • Independent TypeScript generation functions.

  • PowerShell command templates.

  • No dependencies on React or UI components.

Output layer

  • Command preview.

  • Copy individual commands.

  • Copy complete command sets.

  • Export generated commands as a .ps1 file.

4. Migration configuration

The application must support two independently configured domains.

Each domain should eventually support:

  • Domain identifier.

  • Domain distinguished name.

  • File server root path.

  • Target OU hierarchy.

Use fictional example values only.

5. Dynamic folder hierarchy

The user must be able to specify how many folder levels are required.

Requirements:

  • Allow the user to add and remove folder levels.

  • Generate the corresponding input fields dynamically.

  • Allow each level to have an editable label.

  • Maintain the order of the hierarchy.

  • Capture the folder name at each level.

  • Generate a complete folder path from the configured levels.

Do not hard-code five folder levels.

The underlying data structure should be an ordered array rather than a fixed collection of properties.

6. Dynamic OU hierarchy

The OU hierarchy must be independently configurable from the folder hierarchy.

Requirements:

  • Allow the user to add and remove OU levels.

  • Allow each level to have an editable label.

  • Maintain parent-to-child ordering.

  • Generate a Distinguished Name (DN) from the hierarchy.

  • Append the appropriate domain DN.

  • Use the bottom-level OU as the target location for subsequent Active Directory object generation.

We are only interested in the bottom-level target OU for migration operations. We do not need to build a complete Active Directory tree-management tool.

Folder and OU hierarchy depths must not depend on one another.

7. Generation engine

Create a dedicated generation module with clearly defined interfaces.

Initially, implement only generic demonstration functions for:

  • Domain 1 directory creation.

  • Domain 2 directory creation.

Use fictional configuration values.

Do not attempt to recreate company-specific PowerShell commands or naming conventions until their rules have been formally specified and approved.

The generation engine must:

  • Accept structured migration configuration.

  • Produce deterministic PowerShell strings.

  • Keep domain-specific generation rules separate.

  • Be independent of the UI.

  • Be straightforward to extend with additional generators.

8. User interface

Use the supplied reference image as visual guidance.

Design a clean, modern engineering application with:

  • Dark green navigation sidebar.

  • Light main workspace.

  • Clear section headings.

  • Minimal visual clutter.

  • Structured cards for folder and OU configuration.

  • Dynamic hierarchy inputs.

  • Domain configuration.

  • PowerShell preview panel.

The main workflow should be:

  1. Configure migration structure.

  2. Enter migration details.

  3. Preview generated commands.

  4. Export commands.

For Phase 1, the first step and a basic command preview are the priority. Do not build incomplete workflow steps simply for visual effect.

The interface should be responsive and usable on desktop.

9. Scope restrictions

Do NOT implement:

  • AI or LLM integration.

  • PowerShell execution.

  • Active Directory connectivity.

  • Server connectivity.

  • Database persistence.

  • User authentication.

  • Change Request automation.

  • Complex validation.

  • Infrastructure discovery.

  • Automated dependency resolution.

These are outside the scope of Phase 1.

10. Documentation

Create and maintain:

  • PRODUCT_BRIEF.md — application purpose and scope.

  • ARCHITECTURE.md — application layers and component responsibilities.

  • DATA_MODEL.md — migration configuration, domain configuration and hierarchy structures.

  • GENERATION_SPEC.md — generation function contracts and PowerShell template conventions.

  • DECISIONS.md — important architectural decisions and rationale.

  • ROADMAP.md — phased development plan.

11. Development approach

Before implementation:

  1. Inspect the existing repository.

  2. Propose the directory structure.

  3. Explain the proposed data model.

  4. Identify any architectural concerns.

  5. Confirm the implementation sequence.

Then implement the Phase 1 foundation incrementally.

Do not over-engineer.

Write clean, strongly typed, modular code.

Add basic unit tests for hierarchy construction and path/DN generation.

Run the build and tests before declaring the work complete.

Update documentation whenever architectural decisions or implementation details change.

Definition of Done

The application must allow an engineer to:

  1. Configure two domains.

  2. Define an arbitrary folder hierarchy.

  3. Define an independent OU hierarchy.

  4. Enter values at each hierarchy level.

  5. Preview the resulting folder paths and OU Distinguished Names.

  6. Generate basic demonstration PowerShell directory commands.

  7. Copy and export generated commands.

The result should be a functional application foundation ready for additional deterministic PowerShell generation modules.

I'd attach the generated UI reference image to Cursor alongside this prompt.

4. Do we need documentation?

Yes. But I'd keep it lightweight.

Given that we're going to develop this incrementally, documentation will be particularly useful for keeping Cursor aligned with our architectural decisions.

I'd start with these six files:

Document

Purpose

Priority

I wouldn't write these documents independently before development. The prompt instructs Cursor to create them as part of the initial implementation.

We can refine them as the application evolves.

5. My suggested development sequence

  1. Foundation

    Project structure, architecture and documentation.

  2. Dynamic hierarchies

    Folder levels and OU levels, independently configurable.

  3. Domain configuration

    Two domains with independent settings.

  4. Generation engine

    Generic deterministic generators and PowerShell preview.

  5. Export

    Copy commands and download .ps1 files.

One final architectural thought: I would resist adding any more functionality until this foundation works. We have a much bigger opportunity here than simply replacing Excel, but the first objective is to make the basic application work beautifully.

Once that's done, we can introduce the real generation rules as individual, tested modules without having to redesign the application.
